The general form needs additive homomorphism and compatibility with the same left R-scalar action on domain/codomain. Its vector version combines the two laws into one (the usual equivalence follows from T(0)=0). Field vector spaces are unital modules over K, but general R-modules need not be field vector spaces. The source also defines linear operator as a linear map from a module to itself; that is a specialization of domain/codomain, not a third inequivalent general definition. Be cautious that a noncommutative division-ring vector version requires compatible LEFT actions; our admitted field version explicitly restricts scalars to commutative K. No bijection, continuity, injectivity, surjectivity or finite-dimensionality is implied.

formulations.text: Let R be an associative ring and M,N left R-modules. A map T:M→N is R-linear if T(m+m′)=T(m)+T(m′) for all m,m′∈M and T(rm)=rT(m) for every r∈R,m∈M.

formulations.text: Let V,W be vector spaces over the same field K. A map T:V→W is K-linear when T(av+w)=aT(v)+T(w) for every a∈K and v,w∈V.

context: Set-theoretic full image of a total mapping
editorial_screening_reason: ProofWiki directly gives two equivalent formulations for the full set-theoretic image of a mapping: the set of codomain values with a preimage and the image f[S] of the whole domain. These formulations are mathematically identical for a total function, and constitute ONE meaning with two individually traced presentations. They are not the codomain T unless f is surjective, and not the image of an arbitrary subset A unless A=S. The source also presents a class-theoretic extension, which introduces different universe/class-mapping commitments; this broader version is not ingested automatically. The image of a K-linear transformation is a vector subspace, but that additional structure belongs to separately sourced results and is not assumed by this plain mapping definition. Both forms share the same source/target object and are equivalent, not two mathematical meanings.

formulations.text: For a K-linear transformation T:V→W between vector spaces over the same field K, if im(T) is finite-dimensional, its rank is rank(T)=dim_K(im(T)), a finite nonnegative integer.

context: Accumulation point of an indexed topological sequence
editorial_screening_reason: ProofWiki separately defines accumulation of a sequence using INFINITELY MANY indices in every neighborhood, and accumulation of a set by membership in the closure of A minus the queried point. They are not equivalent meanings: a constant sequence may accumulate at its repeated value although the singleton set has no set-accumulation point in a T1 space. Repeated indices matter, not distinct point values. The set formulation is valid in arbitrary topological spaces, with closure relative to X; the sequence formulation requires an indexed infinite sequence and does not imply convergence of its entire sequence. ProofWiki notes cluster point and limit point may use alternative conventions, so do not silently treat those names as identical in every source. Do not impose first countability or metric structure; only topological neighborhoods are used. Sequence accumulation by infinitely many indices and derived-set accumulation of a SET remain different conditions.

formulations.text: For a sequence (x_n) indexed by n∈ℕ in a topological space (X,τ), a point x∈X is a sequence accumulation point if for every open U∈τ containing x, the index set {n∈ℕ:x_n∈U} is infinite.

formulations.text: For A⊆X in a topological space X and x∈X, x is an accumulation point of A if x∈cl_X(A\{x}); equivalently every open neighborhood of x meets A at some point other than x.
